front_blocks.md: Define **compound ion**.

back_blocks.md: A **compound ion** is an ion that contains more than one type of element, such as hydroxide (OH<sup>-</sup>), sulfate (SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>) or nitrate (NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup>).

front_blocks.md: What is the formula of magnesium chloride? Explain how you determine it.

back_blocks.md: The formula is **MgCl**<sub>**2**</sub>. Magnesium (Group 2) has a 2+ charge and chlorine (Group 17) has a 1- charge. Two Cl<sup>-</sup> ions are needed to balance one Mg<sup>2+</sup> ion.

cards.front_md: What is the formula of magnesium chloride? Explain how you determine it.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Ionic compounds are electrically neutral because the total positive charge equals the total negative charge.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
In any ionic compound, the charges from positive and negative ions must balance exactly, giving an overall charge of zero.

front_blocks.md: What is the formula of iron(III) oxide? Explain how you determine it.

back_blocks.md: The formula is **Fe**<sub>**2**</sub>**O**<sub>**3**</sub>. Iron(III) has a 3+ charge and oxygen (Group 16) has a 2- charge. Two Fe<sup>3+</sup> ions (6+) balance three O<sup>2-</sup> ions (6-).

front_blocks.md: Define **Roman numerals in compound names**.

back_blocks.md: **Roman numerals in compound names** are symbols used to indicate the charge (oxidation state) of the metal ion. They are used for transition metals whose charges can vary. For example, copper(II) has a 2+ charge.

Ammonium (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) is an example of a non-metal positive ion.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
Most positive ions are metals, but ammonium (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) and hydrogen (H<sup>+</sup>) are non-metal positive ions.

front_blocks.md: What charges do Group 1, Group 2 and Group 13 metals form when they become ions?

back_blocks.md: **Group 1** metals form **1+** ions, **Group 2** metals form **2+** ions and **Group 13** metals form **3+** ions.

front_blocks.md: Define **spectator ions**.

back_blocks.md: **Spectator ions** are ions present in solution that do not take part in a chemical reaction. They appear on both sides of the full ionic equation and are cancelled out when writing the net ionic equation.

cards.front_md: Define **spectator ions**.
cards.back_md: **Spectator ions** are ions present in solution that do not take part in a chemical reaction. They appear on both sides of the full ionic equation and are cancelled out when writing the net ionic equation.

front_blocks.md: What are the four state symbols used in chemical equations and what do they represent?

back_blocks.md: (s) = **solid**, (l) = **liquid**, (g) = **gas**, (aq) = **aqueous** (dissolved in water).

cards.front_md: What are the four state symbols used in chemical equations and what do they represent?

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
When balancing an equation, you can change the formulae of reactants or products to make the numbers work.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
You must never change the formulae. Only the coefficients (numbers placed in front of formulae) may be changed when balancing an equation.

front_blocks.md: The balanced equation for magnesium burning in oxygen is **..........**  Mg (s) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → **..........**  MgO (s).

back_blocks.md: The balanced equation for magnesium burning in oxygen is **2** Mg (s) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → **2** MgO (s).

front_blocks.md: Define **ionic equation**.

back_blocks.md: An **ionic equation** is a chemical equation showing only the ions and particles that actually take part in a reaction. Spectator ions are omitted and are cancelled from both sides of the full ionic equation.

cards.front_md: Define **ionic equation**.

front_blocks.md: Write the net ionic equation for the reaction of zinc with copper(II) sulfate solution.

back_blocks.md: Zn (s) + Cu<sup>2+</sup> (aq) → Zn<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + Cu (s). The sulfate ion (SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>) is a spectator ion and is cancelled from both sides.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
In a balanced chemical equation, atoms can be created or destroyed as long as the overall mass is conserved.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Atoms cannot be created or destroyed in a chemical reaction. The number of each type of atom must be identical on both sides of the equation.

front_blocks.md: What is the difference between a word equation and a symbol equation?

back_blocks.md: A **word equation** uses only words to show reactants and products. A **symbol equation** uses chemical symbols and formulae to show the number and type of each atom involved in the reaction.

cards.front_md: What is the difference between a word equation and a symbol equation?

front_blocks.md: Define **empirical formula**.

back_blocks.md: An **empirical formula** is the simplest whole-number ratio of the elements present in one molecule or formula unit of a compound. For example, the empirical formula of ethanoic acid (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) is CH<sub>2</sub>O.

cards.front_md: Define **empirical formula**.
cards.back_md: An **empirical formula** is the simplest whole-number ratio of the elements present in one molecule or formula unit of a compound. For example, the empirical formula of ethanoic acid (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) is CH<sub>2</sub>O.

front_blocks.md: How do you calculate the empirical formula from the masses of elements present in a compound?

back_blocks.md: Divide the mass of each element by its **relative atomic mass** to find **moles**. Then divide all values by the smallest to get the **simplest whole-number ratio**.

cards.front_md: How do you calculate the empirical formula from the masses of elements present in a compound?

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Ionic compounds always have the same empirical and molecular formulae.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
Ionic compounds are represented by their simplest formula unit, so their empirical and molecular formulae are always the same.

front_blocks.md: Define **molecular formula**.

back_blocks.md: A **molecular formula** is the exact number of atoms of each element present in one molecule of a compound. For example, ethanoic acid has the molecular formula C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>2</sub>.

cards.front_md: Define **molecular formula**.
cards.back_md: A **molecular formula** is the exact number of atoms of each element present in one molecule of a compound. For example, ethanoic acid has the molecular formula C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>2</sub>.

front_blocks.md: A compound contains 85.7% carbon and 14.3% hydrogen by mass. What is its empirical formula? (A<sub>r</sub>: C = 12.0, H = 1.0)

back_blocks.md: Moles of C = 85.7/12.0 = 7.14. Moles of H = 14.3/1.0 = 14.3. Ratio = 1:2. Empirical formula = **CH**<sub>**2**</sub>.

cards.front_md: A compound contains 85.7% carbon and 14.3% hydrogen by mass. What is its empirical formula? (A<sub>r</sub>: C = 12.0, H = 1.0)

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Organic molecules always have the same empirical and molecular formulae.

back_blocks.md: **False.**

Organic molecules often have different empirical and molecular formulae. For example, ethanoic acid has empirical formula CH<sub>2</sub>O and molecular formula C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>2</sub>.

back_blocks.md: A compound contains 10 g of hydrogen and 80 g of oxygen. The mole ratio of H to O is **2** to **1** giving the empirical formula **H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O**.

front_blocks.md: The empirical formula of compound X is C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>S and its relative formula mass is 180. What is the molecular formula of X? (A<sub>r</sub>: C = 12, H = 1, S = 32)

back_blocks.md: M<sub>r</sub> of empirical formula = (4x12) + (10x1) + 32 = 90. Ratio = 180/90 = 2. Molecular formula = **C**<sub>**8**</sub>**H**<sub>**20**</sub>**S**<sub>**2**</sub>.

front_blocks.md: Define **water of crystallisation**.

back_blocks.md: **Water of crystallisation** is water that is chemically incorporated into the crystal structure of a compound. It is shown in the formula by a dot, e.g. CuSO<sub>4</sub>•5H<sub>2</sub>O.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
A hydrated compound contains water of crystallisation as part of its structure.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
A hydrated compound incorporates water molecules into its crystal lattice. An anhydrous compound contains no water of crystallisation.

front_blocks.md: How can you convert a hydrated salt to its anhydrous form, and how is this reversed?

back_blocks.md: **Heating** the hydrated salt drives off the **water of crystallisation** to give the **anhydrous** compound. Adding water reverses the process, reforming the hydrated salt.

front_blocks.md: Define **anhydrous compound**.

back_blocks.md: An **anhydrous compound** is a compound that contains no water of crystallisation. It is the form obtained when a hydrated salt is fully dried by heating.

cards.front_md: Define **anhydrous compound**.

front_blocks.md: Describe the experimental steps used to determine the degree of hydration (water of crystallisation) of a hydrated salt.

back_blocks.md: Measure the mass of the **hydrated salt** before heating. Heat until **constant mass** is achieved. Calculate the mass of water lost, then use **mole ratios** (dividing by respective M<sub>r</sub> values) to find the number of water molecules.

A compound can only be hydrated to one fixed degree.

front_blocks.md: How is a water of crystallisation calculation similar to an empirical formula calculation?

back_blocks.md: Both involve dividing masses by **formula masses** to find **moles**, then dividing by the smallest value to get the **simplest ratio**. In water of crystallisation calculations the salt and water replace the individual elements.
